title: Tyriq Plummer - YASDery Loves Company: Multiplayer in Traditional Roguelikes
speaker: Tyriq Plummer
summary: Tyriq Plummer argues that party-based multiplayer is an under-explored space for traditional roguelikes, which descend from social tabletop RPGs yet are almost always single-player. He presents two local 2-4 player experiments: HVNTRS (a 2018 7DRL) with queued simultaneous turns, streamlined deterministic play and friendly fire, and Clean Sweep, which introduces a 'parallel asynchronous schedule' where each monster syncs its turns to the most relevant player. He closes with lessons from letting Twitch chat control monsters in Clean Sweep.

insights.claim: Party-based multiplayer is an under-explored space for traditional roguelikes, even though Rogue's tabletop RPG inspirations centre on teamwork and human interaction.
insights.detail: Plummer notes JRPGs and first-person dungeon crawlers kept the adventuring party even as single-player games, but roguelikes did not; a lone delver hungry for godlike power is more like a supervillain than a hero.
insights.quote: I feel like party based Roguelike is an under explored space yearning to be more investigated

insights.claim: Multiplayer roguelikes generate richer stories than solo deaths: betrayal, revenge and tragedy between players, which a real human supplies more cheaply than simulated relationships.
insights.detail: Plummer gives examples: a companion stealing a vital potion and leaving you, hunting them down for revenge, or both ending up cornered. He suggests replacing a relationship simulation (citing Jim Shepard's 2019 talk) with an actual human could save code.
insights.quote: Multi players provides stories of betrayal as your companion steals a vital potion and leaves you to your fate

insights.claim: Playing with a companion makes players more tolerant of a roguelike's difficulty and failure and eases newcomers in, since a partner can teach mechanics hands-on.
insights.detail: Plummer says he learned from Catacomb Kids that people are more tolerant of failure when they have someone to fail with and more inclined to keep trying with a companion, rather than relying on wiki pages.
insights.quote: people are more tolerant of failure and difficulty if they have something to fail along with them

insights.claim: Human party members can engage a roguelike's full system complexity in ways AI allies cannot and that would be tedious for one player controlling several units.
insights.detail: Plummer imagines the wild character builds of Caves of Qud paired with a second, equally complex character built and operated intelligently to support and synergise.
insights.quote: you can really dig into the meat of certain systems in ways that would be inconceivable with AI-based allies

insights.claim: MAngband and its descendant TomeNET are early online multiplayer roguelikes that go real-time but offset the speed demands with input macros while keeping full old-school depth.
insights.detail: Players pick a server and interact with anyone on it. Plummer thinks the macros are invaluable at higher levels and that depth and complexity are not diminished. He contrasts them with the stripped-down Dungeon of the Rogue Daemons.
insights.quote: both games make concessions by being real-time but to alleviate the burden of doing quick mental acrobatics

insights.claim: Plummer's three goals for multiplayer turn design: no timers pressuring decisions, no player waiting ages on others, and multiplayer that actually matters rather than parallel solo play.
insights.detail: Avoiding long waits means limiting the decision space so choices can be made quickly and are easy to input. Making multiplayer matter means encouraging collaboration and risk-taking on behalf of others.
insights.quote: two turns shouldn't make other players wait for ages. This might seem contradictory but it means I want to limit the decision space

insights.claim: HVNTRS has each player queue an action and resolves the turn once all players have chosen, which makes coordination easy and keeps everyone engaged.
insights.detail: Plummer says multiple brains mulling the best move narrows options and speeds things up. Drawbacks: turn order still matters (two players entering the same tile, a move before or after a shield bash), so clear priority rules are needed, and waiting for all inputs is irritating in low-stakes moments like backtracking.
insights.quote: having each player input action to cue it up for execution and as soon as every player has decided on the action the turn resolves

insights.claim: To keep simultaneous turns short, HVNTRS is deterministic with no dice, has no menus, puts every action within two button presses, and hides no information.
insights.detail: Plummer did not want one player allocating skills or navigating menus while others wait. Everything needed to assess a situation is visible on screen, which also makes the game welcoming to new players.
insights.quote: no action in the game is further than two button presses away. You never have to navigate a menu or read anything

insights.claim: Friendly fire in HVNTRS was meant to encourage communication about positioning but may simply be unpleasant in an already tough game.
insights.detail: Weapons like the axe and spear hit multiple tiles, so standing in the wrong place gets you hit by an ally. Plummer concedes it might be overkill in a genre already known for difficulty.
insights.quote: I am definitely concede that friendly fire might actually just suck in practice especially in a game that's already dang tough

insights.claim: Items that need setup and payoff, such as tools to move allies, are of little use alone but become valuable in a team, which better encourages cooperation than friendly fire.
insights.detail: Plummer says such items let players think ahead together and make otherwise unwanted actions interesting in team play; HVNTRS only scratches the surface. It also has a bleed-out timer.
insights.quote: items that beget setup and pay off. These are the items that enable players to think ahead

insights.claim: Clean Sweep's 'parallel asynchronous schedule' has each creature advance its turn only when its most relevant player acts, so players act independently without waiting on or rushing each other.
insights.detail: Plummer's goal was to allow more complexity (bigger inventories, careful scrutiny) without making others wait. Each enemy, after spotting a player, syncs to that player's actions. It works well when players are far apart or separated by walls.
insights.quote: Creatures don't need to care about whose turn it is on a global scale just whose turn it is on the most relevant scale

insights.claim: In Clean Sweep a creature picks its relevant player by line of sight, proximity (stepping adjacent steals attention) and activity (switch to a visible nearby player who has taken more actions than the current target).
insights.detail: Breaking line of sight unsyncs a creature so it can target someone else. The activity rule means if one player idles while another moves and uses items nearby, the monster goes after the active one.
insights.quote: If a player steps adjacent to the player it becomes the target and the closer the player is the more likely to draw the attention

insights.claim: Forcing a monster to switch attention in a parallel schedule is probably exploitable, so a game using it should be designed around those exploits as tactics rather than retrofitted onto an existing roguelike.
insights.detail: Plummer doubts the system can be dropped into an established roguelike with good results, but would welcome someone trying.
insights.quote: you would design the game around exploits and maybe instead of exploits you could call them tactics

insights.claim: Clean Sweep lets any action be queued to fire with the next player's action, enabling combo attack bonuses, push speed boosts, and catching thrown items, which produced comeback moments.
insights.detail: Striking an enemy simultaneously gives an attack bonus; being pushed in your direction of travel gives speed; standing still with a queued action catches thrown items, a fun alternative to dropping or menu trading. Plummer recalls a friend tossing him a healing item when surrounded and near death.
insights.quote: if you cue up an action and stand still you will catch any item any player throws at you

insights.claim: Letting Twitch chat control monsters in Clean Sweep showed that visuals must be readable by drop-in viewers, chat ideally needs its own view to plan surprises, and 'minimal viable fun' is not minimal.
insights.detail: Plummer calls the Twitch integration probably the game's biggest failure. Chat players unfamiliar with roguelike conventions need visual clarity; they cannot do smart things if always in the player's view; and they need many systems and stakes beyond reducing player HP.
insights.quote: the minimal viable fun may not be minimal. You need to do interesting and useful things than just chasing and hurting the player
